---
title: "Validation and the likelihood surface"
author: "Simon Frost"
engine: julia
---

## Overview

The paper fits the model to the survey of 2008–2019 and holds back 2020–2023 to test it.
This vignette reproduces that test at the paper's best parameter set (Table 4), maps the
forecast, and draws the likelihood on a regular grid, PEOC's actions 5 and 8.

```{julia}
using AshDieback
using Plots
```

## The best parameter set

The paper's θmax (eq. 14) is the sample of its AMIS run with the highest likelihood:

```{julia}
data = load_peoc_data()
θmax = AshDiebackParameters(; r_symp = 1000.0, r_allee = 0.0, beta_0 = 23.26, beta_1 = 0.0,
                            D = 18.51, S_sat = 92.0, gamma = 21.50001, C_pers = 1.0,
                            C_init = 0.00855, kappa = 0.056)
prob = AshDiebackProblem(data, θmax)
loglikelihood(prob)
```

## Forecasting beyond the fit

Changing `final_year` extends the simulation with the observed climate. Nothing is refitted:

```{julia}
forecast = remake(prob; settings = ModelSettings(; final_year = 2023))
sol = solve(forecast)
plot(plot(sol; year = 2019), plot(sol; year = 2023); layout = (1, 2), size = (900, 380),
     clims = (0, 1))
```

## Table 4

`rmse` compares each plot visit with the probability of symptoms in its quadrat, each year
and cumulatively:

```{julia}
t = rmse(sol)
```

All of these are within one unit in the fourth decimal of the paper's table. Two differ in
that digit: the cumulative value for 2012 (0.1952 against 0.1951) and the RMSE of 2020 (0.3070
against 0.3071). The printed θmax is rounded, so such differences are to be expected. The paper's
table also has one more plot in 2020 and in 2021 than the released data. The years from 2020 were
not used in the fit, and the error rises there, as the paper reports.

```{julia}
plot(t.years, [t.annual t.cumulative]; label = ["year" "cumulative from 2008"],
     marker = :circle, xlabel = "year", ylabel = "RMSE")
vline!([2019.5]; label = "end of the fit", linestyle = :dash, color = :gray)
```

## The likelihood on a grid

`likelihood_grid` evaluates the log-likelihood on a Cartesian product of parameter values,
holding the rest at their values in the problem. It uses threads when Julia has them. Here
are β₀ and D, the strongly correlated pair:

```{julia}
grid = likelihood_grid(prob, (; beta_0 = range(18, 30; length = 7),
                              D = range(15, 22; length = 8)))
best_parameters(grid)
```

```{julia}
plot(grid; x = :beta_0, y = :D, title = "log-likelihood")
```

The ridge from high β₀ and low D to low β₀ and high D is the correlation of −0.97 in the
paper's Table 3: more spores are offset by slower diffusion.

With more than two axes, `plot` shows the profile, maximised over the others, and
`profile_likelihood` returns it. PEOC's own grid (`peoc_grid_axes()`) has 630 000 points, which
is several hours' work on one machine.
